title: Madison’s two new area plans would require state cooperation - The Capital Times
text: Stoughton Road, which is part of U.S. 51, is pictured at the intersection of Pflaum Road in Madison. The Beltline, Highways 12/18, is pictured from a birds’ eye view. The southeast plan recommends redesigning Stoughton Road to promote mixed-use development. Potential Beltline expansion would affect the southwest plan.  Stoughton Road, which is part of U.S. 51, is pictured at the intersection of Pflaum Road in Madison. The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Madison’s City Council has unanimously approved two new area plans , but with a major question mark at the center of its vision for the southeast and some uncertainty in the southwest because of pending state transportation decisions. With the approval of the two documents — meant to guide decisions around growth, development, infrastructure, business, programs and investment — the city has now completed plans for four of the 12 areas, with planning for downtown Madison underway . Planning for the southeast area began in late 2024, and the adopted plan contains two alternative ideas for the future of the area, depending on the outcome of the state Department of Transportation’s ongoing Stoughton Road study . For city leaders, the stakes of that decision are high. “We have a once in a generation opportunity to get this right and to reshape the east side,” said Ald. Sean O’Brien, who represents the city’s far southeast side, including the eastern side of Stoughton Road. The DOT is considering multiple options for the future shape of the road. The majority would leave the state highway’s current configuration largely unchanged, with lower speed limits, changes to intersections and improved pedestrian infrastructure. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. Under those cases, the land use around Stoughton Road would remain largely unchanged, with commercial and industrial zoning dominating both sides of the highway. But one option — the city’s preferred layout — would see the road become an “urban wide boulevard” between Buckeye Road and Tompkins Drive. That option would have 35 mph speed limits, potential green space or a wide median and connections or full intersections at Allis Avenue, Hob Street, Helgeson Drive and Tompkins Drive. O’Brien likened the design to “East Wash(ington Avenue), but better.” “It could really unlock significant new development that could only make these neighborhoods better, more accessible and more livable, and add housing and all of the things that we'd like to see,” planner and co-project manager Rebecca Cnare said at the city’s June Transportation Commission meeting. “If the road maintains its way as a 45 mile per hour limited access, we don't see much change.” Cnare added that the city’s “very back of the envelope” math shows the potential for hundreds of millions of dollars in economic development along Stoughton Road. City Council members argued the design would be the biggest improvement in terms of traffic safety. Southeast Ald. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford said she was “particularly hopeful” that Stoughton Road would be redesigned into a wide boulevard to ensure La Follette High School students “are safe and able to cross the street.” The design could also promote more bus service in the southeast area. A perceived lack of transit options in the southeast area was residents’ second most-common transportation concern in a survey last year, with unsafe intersections as the No. 1 issue. The plan notes Madison Metro Transit routes run along the area’s major east-west corridors like Cottage Grove, Buckeye and Pflaum Roads via the C, D and L lines, but north-south service along South Stoughton Road and farther east are lacking. Accordingly, the plan calls for the city to “support options that could enable a future bus rapid transit route” in the Stoughton Road redesign, an idea O’Brien said could be “transformative” for the area. Still, public opinion on the Stoughton Road alternatives has been split, Cnare said, and the boulevard option could entail longer drive times. She argued the potential benefits would outweigh potential congestion and more stops for drivers. “That's OK when you're talking about a living, breathing neighborhood,” Cnare said. Transportation Commission member Robbie Webber also expressed concern the state would be “pretty resistant” to the city’s preferred option. The final call on the new design, however, is in the state’s hands, and Cnare and O’Brien both said they’re waiting for a decision just like everyone else. “It has been a conversation that's been happening for decades, possibly since even before I was born,” O’Brien said. “I am willing to consider a lot of options to make sure that we get the Stoughton Road design that we need.” Pending state decisions about highway projects will also affect the implementation of transportation plans in Madison’s southwest. The state Department of Transportation is studying whether to expand the Beltline between Middleton and Verona Road to improve traffic along the major corridor, with options including a full-time general purpose lane or a flex lane. Under a maximal scenario, 77 residences, including 13 single-family homes and apartments, would be demolished, and the state is also looking to improve traffic flow along Verona Road. The Beltline, Highways 12/18, is pictured from a birds’ eye view. The city has opposed Beltline expansion, citing concerns about pollution and further dividing neighborhoods. But as it studies whether to expand the highway, the Department of Transportation is also considering adding more Beltline crossings for cars, bikes and pedestrians, including one between Gammon Road and Whitney Way, and a shared-use path from the Southwest Path to the West Towne Path north of the Beltline. “While these components would be beneficial to the Southwest Area and the city, they would not offset the overall detriment that the Beltline project represents if interchange and general purpose lane expansion is undertaken,” the city's southwest plan says. Madison’s plan calls for the city to “partner with” the state transportation agency to make improvements at Beltline interchanges. The plan also envisions realigning Schroeder Road to reduce conflict points near the highway and Whitney Way and new street connections across the Beltline — more than are contained in the state’s study process. Ben Zellers, city planner and project co-manager, said the plan was meant to reflect the city’s wishes for transportation plans in the area as it waits for a final decision from the state Department of Transportation. “There's a concern that (the state) may propose something that further exacerbates many of the issues that are there right now,” Zellers told the Transportation Commission this month. “This plan identifies the city's desire to move in a different direction.” Will Briggs is the housing and transportation reporter for the Cap Times. Will writes about housing, transportation, development and more related to growth in the Madison region. Email story ideas and tips to wbriggs@captimes.com . title: Wisconsin tourism sets records for fourth consecutive year
text: Madison Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes Resize: Fans crowd around the draft stage during the second round of the NFL football draft, Friday, April 25, 2025, in Green Bay, Wis. (AP Photo/Matt Ludtke)  Digital Content Manager   Fans crowd around the draft stage during the second round of the NFL football draft, Friday, April 25, 2025, in Green Bay, Wis. (AP Photo/Matt Ludtke) MADISON, Wis. -- More people are visiting Wisconsin than ever before, and its becoming a boon for the state. The Wisconsin Department of Tourism said Tuesday that tourism to the state generated $27 billion in total economic impact in 2025, or roughly $74 million per day. That's Wisconsin's fourth consecutive year of record-breaking tourism in a row, topping the $25.8 billion of economic impact generated in 2024. Wisconsin saw a record number of visits in 2025 with 117.9 million visits tallied, up 3.5 million from the previous record. Tourism generated over $1.7 billion in state and local revenue, another record. "These numbers are a big deal for our state, our economy, and the countless hardworking folks in the industry who make it all happen," Evers said. "W e will keep uplifting this essential industry and the dedicated folks that drive it to ensure travel and tourism in Wisconsin continues to grow and thrive for future generations." Record tourism was driven in part by record attendance at EAA AirVenture and the Northern Wisconsin State Fair in Chippewa Falls as well as the 2025 NFL Draft in Green Bay. The record-breaking growth included Dane County. Destination Madison said a record 9.65 million people visited Madison and the county in 2025 and spent $1.6 billion. Visitor spending in Madison and Dane County averaged $4.5 million per day, and direct visitor spending increased across all categories including lodging, retail and recreation and entertainment. "Madison is a welcoming city that’s teeming with events and destinations enjoyed by all," Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said. "Our hospitality staff make everyone feel like they belong and that every visit is memorable." ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. title: Jim Troupis Says He Cant Get Fair Trial in Madison » Urban Milwaukee
text: Faces 11 criminal counts of forgery for 2020 false electors scheme, wants a change of venue. Jim Troupis, a Republican attorney and former judge, center, makes his initial appearance in court Dec. 12, 2024, at the Dane County Courthouse in Madison, Wis. Troupis, Kenneth Chesebro and Michael Roman were arraigned for charges related to their roles in the 2020 fake elector scheme that aimed to overturn Donald Trump’s Wisconsin loss to Joe Biden. (Joe Timmerman / Wisconsin Watch) Attorneys for Jim Troupis , who served as President Donald Trump ’s 2020 Wisconsin campaign lawyer, are arguing that Troupis cannot receive a fair trial in Madison. They’re asking for his criminal trial to be moved out of Dane County . In briefs filed to the court on Tuesday, Troupis’ attorneys also argued that one of his felony forgery charges should be dropped, because Troupis — along with dozens of other people involved in Trump’s efforts to overturn the outcome of his failed second bid for the White House — received a federal pardon. Troupis faces 11 criminal counts of forgery for his role in developing the false electors scheme, in which Republican delegates for Trump in Wisconsin and other swing states submitted official-looking documentation attesting that Trump had won their states, even though he had lost. Troupis and former Trump campaign attorney Ken Chesebro , who will also stand trial in Wisconsin, have been accused of developing that scheme, using Wisconsin as a testing ground . They argue that they were maintaining all of Trump’s legal avenues while his challenges to state outcomes moved through various courts. The Wisconsin Department of Justice brought criminal charges against Troupis, Chesebro and Mike Roman , a 2020 Trump campaign aide, in 2024. These briefs are Troupis’ team’s latest efforts to move off the trial, after a judge in December found probable cause for the case against him to move forward. They’d previously argued that the judge presiding over the case had engaged in misconduct . That argument was unsuccessful. In one brief , Troupis’ attorneys argued that the publicity that has surrounded the case for the last half-decade has irreparably hurt Troupis’ ability to get a fair trial. They argue that Dane County public figures including state Supreme Court justices and Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes Conway disparaged Troupis, and that local media has tainted public opinion. It also argues that the state Department of Justice’s argument, that Troupis’ actions harmed all Wisconsin voters whose ballots were challenged , would mean that nearly every eligible Dane County juror counts as a victim of Troupis’ alleged crimes. “This case is headed to trial. No question. Neither side is going to blink. And when we get to trial, Troupis has the right to a fair and impartial jury,” reads the brief. “To make sure that he has that, the jurors must be free of bias and contempt, they can’t be victims and they can’t identify with them. That, plus provocative and emotionally-charged pretrial publicity, necessitates a change of venue.” In the other brief , Troupis’ lawyers say that one of the 11 counts against him should be dropped, because he was on a recent Trump pardon list of people involved in the false electors scheme. Chesebro and Roman were also on that list. Federal pardons have no impact on state investigations. But in the brief, Troupis’ lawyers say that the document that the false electors signed was a real document, not a forgery. It also argues that the state cannot prosecute over the casting of electoral votes, because that is a federal process — and, therefore, Trump’s pardon does apply here. The other 10 criminal counts are tied to each of the 10 false electors, whom prosecutors allege were defrauded by Troupis, Chesebro and Roman. Those electors previously settled a civil lawsuit against them for signing those documents in December of 2020, in which they admitted that their actions were “part of an attempt to improperly overturn the 2020 presidential election results.” Troupis and Chesebro also separately settled that civil lawsuit . title: Candidates for Francesca Hong's Assembly seat explain their views - The Capital Times
text: Candidates for Wisconsin's 76th Assembly District participate in a candidate forum at Garver Feed Mill on Wednesday, June 17, 2026, in Madison, Wis. The event, hosted by the SASY Neighborhood Association, Williamson Marquette Business Alliance and Indivisible Madison East, featured a community meet-and-greet and discussion of issues facing the district. The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. The Democratic candidates vying for a state Assembly seat representing much of Madison’s east side vary in professional backgrounds and on some policy issues, such as how to expand state support for housing affordability. The five candidates do, however, agree on several issues, such as funding public schools and who they support in the race for Wisconsin’s next governor. District 76 in the Assembly has been represented by Francesca Hong since 2021. This fall, Hong is among seven Democratic candidates seeking to succeed Gov. Tony Evers. At a forum June 17 for the District 76 candidates, Isaia Ben-Ami, Juliana Bennett, Tony Castañeda, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford and Zoe Sullivan discussed their qualifications and policy priorities. Taxes, private school vouchers, conservation funding, election maps and state aid for local government were among the subjects candidates focused on. Ben-Ami introduced himself as a lifelong Madisonian, a career policy professional and state Legislature veteran aide. His platform focuses on his experience in transportation and housing policy. Bennett is a former City Council member, a housing advocate and a University of Wisconsin-Madison alum. At the forum, she emphasized her desire to “fight fascism” and the Trump administration and continue advocating for affordable housing. Castañeda described his background as a Racine native, highlighting his parents' involvement in the Mexican American community and his activism in social movements, such as the fight for Chicano studies at UW-Madison in the 1970s and the anti-apartheid movement in South Africa. Martinez-Rutherford is a small business owner, food service worker and City Council member who represents part of Madison’s east side. Sullivan talked about her background as a journalist and organizer, and “holding politicians accountable.” She touted her reporting on the environmental impact of data centers and for building coalitions among stakeholders in the community. The forum was hosted by the SASY Neighborhood Association and the Williamson Marquette Business Alliance, and moderated by the Isthmus. Candidates discussed the importance of addressing regulatory concerns over data centers, housing affordability, public school funding and the potential for Democratic control of state government in Wisconsin. The candidates said they supported clean energy initiatives, working-class families, teachers and service industry workers. They said many vulnerable groups of voters are feeling left behind by state and federal Democratic leaders. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. The candidates unanimously said they support Hong for governor. They talked about furthering the Democratic Party’s values, but many emphasized the role their personal identities play in their politics. Martinez-Rutherford said she identifies as a Democratic Socialist because she wants to build coalitions and ensure stakeholders have seats at the table. “I build relationships, and I live in community, and it's our duty to make sure that we're working together for the betterment of the people of Wisconsin,” she said. “When it comes to it, I have a backbone. I can stand up when I believe that something is right, and I will stand up when our Democratic coalition decides that negotiating the dignity of working people is acceptable.” Bennett said she’s proud to be the only candidate endorsed by the Madison-area Democratic Socialists of America and for striving to be the first queer, Black woman elected to the Assembly. “Our campaign team is organized in Darbo and Kennedy Heights, in the mobile home park, in Vera Court, in Northport Apartments, and they haven't met a politician ever,” Bennett said. “I don't know where my opponents are all the time, but I know that I am very grateful to be the first person to knock on their door, and what matters is that we fight for those people who say their top concern is having baby formula, diapers, canned food goods and basic human needs.” Asked when they would break from Democratic Party values, many candidates focused on reaching voices less heard by legislators. Castañeda mentioned his Chicano heritage and the importance of justice. “Chicano politics are about community. They're working-class politics. They're about working-class analysis. They're about fairness, and they're about justice, and that's what I stand for,” he said. “I also feel that there will be struggles with some people in the Democratic Party, but I think that I am able to reach and talk to these people, and especially if we get the majority, we have got to be unified but not only that. I'm not afraid and unwilling, and I know I'm very able to also talk to a lot of Republicans.” Sullivan brought up her role as a journalist in how she would approach the role. “I have talked with lots of people from many different political perspectives, and I think that is one of the qualities that I would bring to this position, which is that I can really sit and listen to just about anybody,” she said. Ben-Ami said lawmakers should think in terms of operating under a split government to get work done, adding “you have to be willing to be at the table and know when to step away when it's quite clear that those decisions are going to go against your values.” “I also describe myself as a Democrat, because it is a political coalition that you will need to earn the votes of at least 51 members of the Assembly and at least 33 members of the Senate to be able to actually get things done, you have to move policy forward,” he said. “I think that we need to go full heart into changing this economy, so it's not benefiting the few and actually helping the many.” The five candidates agreed on needing more than a moratorium on new development of data centers, increased funding for clean climate and energy projects, and support for municipal clerks administering elections.
